noi_dung:
Rules of the Chan Session

In 1959, the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association was founded. Its predecessor was the Sino-American Buddhist Association. From its founding until now, every year the Association has held many Buddha-recitation Sessions and Chan Sessions; yet those Sessions have all been conducted in silence, so very few people know that Buddha-recitation Sessions or Chan Sessions are held at Gold Mountain Monastery. That is because we do not advertise or seek publicity, nor do we seek after external conditions—we simply cultivate genuinely. If anyone hears that a Chan Session is being held and wishes to join, they are still welcome. But we absolutely do not solicit or call on others for support, saying: "Gold Mountain Monastery is holding a Session, and there are several 'no-mind cultivators' practicing there. Come make offerings and your merit will be limitless." From the beginning until now, we have never trumpeted ourselves that way!

In China, whenever a Chan Session is held, the offerings from donors can cover expenses for a whole year, sometimes with surplus besides. During a Session, a great many laypeople resolve to make offerings to form good affinities, supplying the monastery with goods such as rice, noodles, oil, soy sauce, dried foods, and so on.

In America, Buddhism is still in its infancy, so we must transform the mistakes of the past and head toward perfection. There is a saying: "A good beginning is half the work done." We do not use tactics to gain offerings. Had we used the tactics and methods used in China, we might have been more successful!

Why do we not seek offerings? Because first of all we must cultivate sincerely and accord with the arrangement of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. When the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, the eightfold division of gods and dragons, and the Dharma-protecting good spirits see us applying effort in cultivating the Way, they will naturally bring about sympathetic response. If we do not cultivate genuinely, then even if people come to make offerings, we should feel deeply ashamed, for:

If the three minds are not ended, even water is hard to digest;

If the Five Contemplations are understood, even gold is easily digested.

(If the past, present, and future minds are not ended, then even a glass of water offered by a donor cannot be digested.

But if the principle of the Five Contemplations is understood, then even gold and iron are easily digested.)

If we have not yet severed the three minds (the past mind, the present mind, and the future mind), then even a glass of water offered by a donor cannot be digested. But if we clearly understand the principle of the Five Contemplations, then even gold and iron are easily digested. What are the Five Contemplations?

Reflect on how much labor went into producing this bowl of rice.

Consider whether your own virtue is complete or deficient in accepting this offering.

Guard your mind, keeping it far from error, whose roots are greed, anger, and delusion.

Regard food as medicine, taking it to cure the withering of the body.

Accept this food only in order to accomplish the karma of the Way.

Tonight the Chan Session begins. The Chan Session at our Gold Mountain Monastery is very different from Chan Sessions in monasteries in China. Their Chan Sessions are really "eating sessions," because every night they eat steamed buns! Even Gold Mountain Monastery in Zhenjiang and Gaomin Monastery in Yangzhou are no exception. A great many meditators make a point of attending Sessions at monasteries that serve evening buns. Wherever the buns are good, they go. They do not judge the quality of the Chan Session, only whether the buns are big or small, tasty or bland. Thus some monasteries are famous for their big, delicious, fragrant buns. I say this with no intent to slander monastics who cannot let go of food and drink—it is simply that such things really happen.

This Gold Mountain Monastery has no custom of eating buns—not even a small bite for a snack.

In China, during a Chan Session a great many laypeople come to make offerings to the meditators. After one hour of sitting, a layperson comes to offer four longans. After the next sitting, someone else offers two peanut candies or a piece of pastry. In short, after every hour of Chan someone comes with offerings, stirring greed in those "mindless cultivators," who eat until their bellies bulge and can no longer sit still. At this monastery such things will not happen; that is the difference.

Each morning, sitting begins at two-thirty, followed by walking meditation—continuously until midnight, when we rest. You must practice asceticism, train bitterly. You must do what no one else can do. But if you do not hang the two words "birth and death" before your eyes, and instead complain you haven't slept enough, then sit there entering the "sound-sleep samadhi"—if that is how it is, you will never accomplish anything.

You must join the Session "heedless of death, forgetting life." You must truly apply effort in the Session. You must reap the results you are meant to reap—only then is it of use. Do not "drift with the waves," doing whatever others do. Seeing someone sit, you sit; seeing someone sleep, you sleep—that will not do; it only wastes time and does you no good at all.

In the past I joined Chan Sessions in many places. Nowhere was I ever struck by the incense monitor (the one who patrols and strikes drowsy meditators awake with a stick). Why? Because I never dozed off. By day I sat in the Chan Hall, by night I also sat in the Chan Hall—all twenty-four hours of the day I sat in the Chan Hall, knowing nothing of rest or snoring. Not even a second did I waste—at every moment I applied the skill I had to apply, at every moment I kept my skill raised up.

All of you here are people of deep good roots, intelligent, possessed of wisdom. You must treat this cultivation as truly important; do not go through the motions. In this Chan Session, someone must become enlightened. If no one becomes enlightened, then when the Session ends, each of you will take a beating of a hundred blows! If you feel you can bear a hundred blows, then you need not become enlightened; if you cannot bear it, then strive to become enlightened! If anyone fears a beating, right now, before the Session begins, you may withdraw! Once you have joined, you must stay from beginning to end—no quitting halfway. By the rule of the Chan Hall, you have already bid farewell to life and death—if anyone dies, the corpse is simply tucked beneath the sitting bench and may not be carried outside. All the more, when no one has died, you may not quit halfway.

Right here you must draw the line between life and death. If not alive, then dead; if not dead, then alive:

Unable to cast aside death, you cannot exchange it for life.

Unable to cast aside the false, you cannot realize the true.

(If you cannot throw away death, you cannot trade it for life.

If you cannot throw away the false, you cannot realize the true.)

That is the threshold of Gold Mountain Monastery. So in this year's Chan Session, you must be utterly vigorous. No matter what, you must recognize your own "original face." If you do not recognize your "original face," no one may think of slipping out Gold Mountain Monastery's great gate! If you sneak away, you will be "put in prison"! That, roughly, is the rule of this year's Chan Session; I hope you will all comply!

(Explained on January 6, 1974, at Gold Mountain Monastery, San Francisco)
